analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "In a minute, we'll hear arguments next in Montana against the United States. Thank you. Mr. Poore, I think you may proceed whenever you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. This is an appeal by the state of Montana from the majority judgment of a three-judge federal district court declaring that the Montana contractor's gross receipts tax is unconstitutional as to the government and those with whom it deals on the grounds that it violates the Supremacy Clause in that the proceeds of the Act, which is a state act, of course, flow to the state of Montana and not to the federal government, and therefore there is discrimination against the federal government. Of course, for an understanding of the lower court's holding, it is necessary to also understand the act in question, which imposes a 1% gross receipts tax on any public contractor who has a job above $1,000 in the state of Montana. Thus, a contractor who would be building a road for the state of Montana or a contractor building a road for a dam for the federal government, and this is important to us, a contractor who would be building a school for a school district in Butte or building a dam for private landowners who had organized a public irrigation district as authorized by Montana statute, or building a sewage lagoon for the benefit of private citizens who have organized a sewage disposal district, and on and on as to the various sub-boards and commissions that are authorized under our Montana Act and generally throughout all of the states, to the best of my knowledge, any such contract for construction, whether it was state, whether it was federal, or whether it was board or commission-oriented, would pay the tax. The tax, however, does not fall upon a private contractor, that is, a contractor doing business for a strictly private individual. It is important also that the court understand the purpose of the act. The need for the act became apparent in Montana in the mid-60s, when, by virtue of the amount of public construction, both state and federal, and the natural mobility of the equipment used in such construction, the various assessing counties in the state found that they were unable to keep track of the heavy equipment used by contractors, and that, to quote the testimony, you might say, of the witnesses at the trial court level, some contractors would claim that their equipment on tax day was in Gallatin County, another would claim that it was, or he would then claim to another county that it was in Cascade County, and to a third that it didn't even exist. I can confirm that to a certain extent. One of my experiences working construction in the middle part of Colorado during summers was loading contractors' equipment onto flat cars and shipping it from one county to another. That's the very problem, Your Honor. And for a while, they used to even drive cattle across state lines. Of course, that isn't applicable here. But the chasing down of equipment and getting it assessed to the proper county and properly assessed was a real problem. Consequently, the incentive for these contractors to properly declare their equipment, and the problem wasn't as pertinent to ordinary private individuals building a home or a garage or a ranch or building a barn, because he was traditionally dealing in his own county with the contractors known to the assessor. But the incentive under the Act then was... Excuse me. Would there not be large private contractors, though, that would have the same kind of problem, say, building a big office building or... Yes, a large private contractor... Again, there aren't that many in Montana, but if the Montana Power Company had it, was going to build a large office building, it probably would, if he was going to build it, it was going to be built in Butte, there probably would be some contractors come from the far ends of the state and therefore get out of their own particular counties, and... would create a similar problem there, Your Honor. How many large buildings does the Montana Power Company have throughout the state? It has one in Butte. When you say large, what do you mean by large? How many stories? Butte's building is four stories high and about 100 feet on the fronting on Broadway Street. And I'm guessing that they have maybe two or three other somewhat comparable buildings throughout the entire state. The incentive for, of course, for the declaration, and there was a purpose behind the act, was not to get at the federal government in any way, shape, or form. Mr. Formey, just to be sure I understand, is it the state's submission that substantially all the large construction projects are public projects? There are, for example, schools and all the rest are the only... I don't... I think that'd be definitely true, that the largest... the larger construction is state construction, like a new law building at the university or building roads and that type of thing. Of course, the federal construction in Montana has been substantial, and the private construction, like the Montana Power, and another name just doesn't jump to me, would be relatively small. Of course, the incentive was a dollar-for-dollar credit, so that the... I think the government uses a happy phrase that this tax was hostage to the payment of personal property taxes and income taxes. By virtue of these credits, the effective rate of the 1% tax becomes one-half of 1%. And in Keywood No. 2, the state of Montana held that this was a valid revenue-producing measure. Now, this act was enacted in 1967. Thereafter, the government, the federal government, which had a contract to build a liby dam with the Keywood and Sons, directed Keywood to file one action in the state courts, which became Keywood No. 1. The federal government itself filed this action in the federal court, as I say, this particular action. Now, it's important that the court understand that these two actions were substantially identical, that the government had directed the filing of the state court action, was stipulated and is stipulated to be the real party in interest, controlled all the strategy of the state court action, and paid all of the costs. As soon as these two actions were filed in April of 1971, the state court action was first, the federal court action shortly thereafter. The three court judges then ordered the hearing on the question of abstention of the tax and an injunction against the state of Montana, and the state of Montana filed a motion for an abstention of the action in the federal court, pending a resolution in the state court, and cited the Meridian case of this Supreme Court. The day that the matter was set for hearing, the government, referring to the federal government, stipulated with the state of Montana for continuance of the lawsuit in the federal court, pending a final resolution in the state courts. Thereafter, the matter did proceed, and I emphasize that the same identical questions, the constitutionality of the act under the Supremacy Clause and under the Equal Protection Clause, were presented in the state court, and it proceeded up through the state court, first in the trial court, tried before a county judge, then affirmed in the state Supreme Court, where the court held that the government was, that the act, more accurately, did not violate the Equal Protection Clause, and it did not violate the Supremacy Clause, which are the two, at least the second one, the issue of the Supremacy Clause, is the viable issue here, unless there are procedural difficulties to that. After the case had been decided by the Montana Supreme Court, the state of Montana then notified the three-judge federal court and moved for a summary judgment. The government then pointed out that it had the right of direct appeal to this court. This was in the spring of 1973, and a notice of appeal was actually filed to this court. As of that time, that this matter had been heard by this court in 1973, the same issues would have been presented, or presentable to this court, as now appear here. Namely, whether or not the act, the Montana Act, does or does not violate the Supremacy Clause. As of that time, however, Fresno had not been decided, but the Duma versus Phillips versus Duma was the law of the land in this aspect. As soon as the notice of appeal to this court was filed, there was another stipulation, again, to continue the matter, and the order of the court was made, the federal court, directing that the matter just be continued until there was a final disposition by appeal to the United States Supreme Court or otherwise. As I say, the appeal was filed, and then the United States, at the direction of the then Solicitor General, Mr. Irwin N. Griswold, directed the dismissal of the appeal. Does the state know why that decision was made? No, Your Honor, the state does not know. I would like to speculate as to why they just wanted, we view very strongly that they wanted another trial, de novo, in the federal court, if they could get it, because of the status of the fact, the matter having been decided adversely to them at that stage. I take it the state of Montana knew all the time that the United States was a real party in interest? Yes, Your Honor, the way that came about is that at the end, I tried the case in the county court. At the end of the case, well, first of all, the court should be apprised that as soon as the state, it appeared that the matter was going to be tried in the state court, the state of Montana moved to strike those allegations in the state action that pertained to the federal government itself, saying that it was irrelevant since Kiewit was the named party in the state court action. That was denied by the trial judge. At the end of the case, I and Mr. Sherman Long, who was then trying the case for Kiewit, I raised the question of real party in interest, and I said, the true real party in interest is the United States government, Sherman Long, Mr. Long. He conceded that, but both of us, to get the matter expedited and proceed on through and have a determination of it, I just agreed that the United States government was a real party in interest, but the matter would proceed under the Kiewit denomination. Who did Mr. Long represent? He represented Kiewit and was paid by the U.S. government. And is it stipulated in the findings or in the agreed statement that he was paid by the U.S. government? Yes, the agreed statement of fact that all costs of the Kiewit litigation were paid by the federal government that determined the strategy, controlled the strategy of the case, and paid all the costs, including costs of appeal. Does the record show that if Kiewit, or that if, yes, if Kiewit had prevailed, whether the United States would have obtained the refund? If Kiewit had prevailed, Your Honor, what? Does the record show that the government would have obtained the refund? If Kiewit had prevailed, then there would have been a, had to have been a refund, of course. To whom? To whom? Well, that is a rather complex question because that case was tried on the Libby Dam contract, and the Libby Dam contract had a Clause 58 that provided that the contractor, namely Kiewit, would not take advantage of the refunds and credits, which was a very strange provision, and then that was withdrawn by the government. But I would say that the refund would have, had to have been paid first to Kiewit, and then I presume that it would have been passed on down to the owner of the property, namely, the United States government. Again, I would like to, in an argumentative sense, point out that I think that the reason that Mr. Solicitor General Griswold directed the dismissal of the action was to endeavor to get a retrial in the federal court system, and as it turned out, it was an advantageous result. But we feel that it was not justified or justifiable that they had by then waived their right to return to the federal court. So after the appeal was dismissed in the summer of 73, the state of Montana again moved for summary judgment and cited the England rule and also raised the questions of collateral estoffel, and the, both of these motions were denied by the federal court below, and the court then proceeded to hear the trial of the case. The lower court held here that under the Fresno County ruling the revenue from the state tax, which goes only to the state of Montana, of course, since it's a state tax, and does not flow over to the federal government, that in itself creates an unconstitutional imbalance in that it violates the supremacy clause. This, of course, is the issue that the amikai curiae are very disturbed about. Yet I don't think it would be possible to read the Fresno County case to study it and justify that particular holding. The lower court also held that the England rule did not bar the relitigation in the federal court, even though that the litigation in the state court covered the same issues as in the federal court and had gone to the portals of the United States Supreme Court before being dismissed and could have been, there could have probable jurisdiction since it was granted in this case, would have been granted in 1973 and the same issues would have been determined by this court and not required a retrial in the federal court. Doesn't England, though, require that the case start out in the federal court and then both parties voluntarily submit their claims to the state court, their state claims and then reserve their federal claims? I don't think, Your Honor, that England requires that the actions start in the federal court. I think the rationale of England is that there is a federal court action and that there are constitutional issues as to which there should be a determination by the state court. And here there was already a week earlier pending action in the state court and I think this court would be interested that in 1965 the state of Montana had thrown out as unconstitutional an earlier act that would be the immediately predecessor act to this. And it was thrown out on the grounds that there was discrimination between in-state and out-of-state contractors. But the Montana Supreme Court recognizing the problem of collection of taxes in Montana had in effect urged or invited the legislature to come up with a constitutional solution to this problem. So this act came up and so it was obviously very ripe for a determination by the Montana Supreme Court as to whether this particular act was or was not constitutional. A second try so to speak. But you're not arguing that the government's agreement for a continuance of the federal court litigation amounted to a stipulation that the federal court should abstain under the England Act. Yes, that's just just what I there again I was the attorney present. We had made our motion for an abstention. We met before the court commenced the hearing that morning and the federal government said we didn't unfortunately use the word abstain. We said it continued but to us it's a matter of semantics. Well, I think that the meaning to me would be quite different. You know, a plaintiff, a defendant could move that a plaintiff's complaint be dismissed 10 days prior to the trial. On trial date you come and stipulate the trial be continued for two months. That isn't the same thing as stipulating that it be dismissed. No, did I say that I'd move to the... No, you say it's semantical as between continuance and agreeing that there should be England doctrine abstention. I didn't mean to say that the government agreed that they would be out of court if by virtue of this continuance we'd automatically apply the England. It all depended on what happened in the state court. But I do believe that the matter was continued to obtain a determination in the state court and it fully complies the mechanics of that agreement fully complies with the doctrine of England because there was a submission of all of the issues by the federal government to the state court for determination. They were in control of the case and they were the real party in interest. Then when it went adversely they sought the return of the federal court and I think that they had as of that time waived the right to return of the federal court under England. The holding of the majority below main point was that the act was unconstitutional as under the very lower court's interpretation of Fresno which we feel was in error. Secondly, they held that the rule of England didn't bar relitigation in the federal court and the lower court also held that the doctrine of collateral of Estoppel doesn't bar relitigation in the federal court. The dissent of Judge Kilkenny of course points up the issues before this court because he felt that there was this grave procedural problem that the doctrine of England had precluded return to the federal court that collateral Estoppel did bar litigation and that the majority had misapplied the Fresno County case. Because of the dialogue between the court and counsel this morning I'll jump over the first procedural question that's raised by England and collateral Estoppel and get into the merits of the case on Fresno that Fresno County was misconstrued by the lower court. We respectfully submit that the doctrine of the holding of Fresno County wholly supports the constitutional validity under the supremacy clause of this Montana Act in question. Of course Fresno is based upon the ancient case McCullough versus Maryland and the rule of Fresno as updated excuse me the rule of McCullough as updated by Dravo which was decided in 1937 and Phillips Chemical in 1960 in Fresno County just less than two years ago stands for the proposition that a state tax with economic impact on the United States is not unconstitutional if the economic impact is not direct and here it was not direct there was no tax upon any instrumentality of the government any property of the government it's not substantial it's a half of one percent and in Dravo it was a two percent tax if the tax is not discriminatory. Do you think counsel that the supremacy clause and what has been referred to in some of our cases is the doctrine of intergovernmental tax immunity are interchangeable? Yes I believe that as soon as there's a question of intergovernmental tax immunity if there's impact on the federal government I think we have a supremacy issue. Well supremacy often involves a preemption supremacy clause is at least broader than intergovernmental tax immunity is it not? Intergovernmental tax immunity might be one aspect of the supremacy clause. Yes my understanding of supremacy is that there cannot that a state cannot take any action which could embarrass the federal government in the proper performance of its functions and any aspect of that in some context different and other things doesn't it? Yes Preemption for example which is not here at all is it? No there's no issue of preemption and that I think brings up the confusion at least of the tax administrators in the western states initially under what did discrimination mean because in 1937 under Dravo just the word bald word discrimination seemed to connote a 14th amendment due process discrimination but Phillips Chemical indicated there was a much broader than that and this court indicated that in cases where there was a potential conflict between the sovereigns or between the sovereign state and nation that the language that would be found in equal protection clauses would not be necessarily controlling fortunately then Fresno County came along and it seems to us that that has clarified at least in this area that we're concerned with here what does discrimination mean where there is a state tax with a potential economic impact upon the federal government of course the initial holding of that case which the lower court didn't apparently recognize is there must be a political check available amongst the constituents of the particular state such that there can't be a ganging up on the federal government such that the state of Montana would have inhibitions in endeavoring to up the tax such that there would be adverse economic impact on the federal government what are the protections against that in our act the important thing is to point out that there are these multitudinous statewide irrigation districts flood control districts soil comfort districts lighting districts I myself my home is subject to a lighting district where private individuals get together organize under allowable state law to create an improvement district for their own properties and then assess or make their own property subject to the repayment of the cost of the improvement now all construction under such districts would be subject to this tax the irrigation district itself would be in precisely the same position as the federal government in its construction of property in other words the contractor building the irrigation district would pay identical tax as the contractor building an irrigation district for the federal government the passed on impact of the tax would be identical to the irrigation district organized by the small group of private property owners as would be the impact on the federal government when you say an irrigation district is organized by a small group of private property when it's organized it becomes a public entity that's exactly right your honor and Montana is 700 miles long and 400 miles wide water is a curse and a blessing we'll have an irrigation district in one part of the state we'll have a flood control district in another on soil we'll have a soil conservation district someplace and something and also we'll have relatively large towns relatively small towns the small towns that have to have water districts they'd have to have sewage districts they have to have lighting districts and of course every town or city has a school district all of these are public entities that are taxed exactly the same upon them as upon the federal government and they are the owners of that district if you will the people who are going to be impacted are private voting citizens of the state of Montana consequently we submit that the required political check that was set forth in the Fresno County case is here in our Montana Act there's no way these are all creatures of the state aren't they no no no no your honor none of them they're not creatures of the state if this court were to organize an irrigation district could be in Gallatin County and the state would have nothing the state the state court the county court would organize that district upon petition of the land owners if the district went broke and couldn't pay for the dam that had been set up then the lien would be on the property of those people who had set up the district and there's no feedback whatever your honor of revenue suppose it were a municipality would your answer be the same yes the municipalities have to rise or fall or stand on their own revenues there's no identification of a municipality with the state of Montana if in the city of Butte we are considering building a new city hall that'll be a perfect example it'll cost the citizens of the city of Butte one half of one percent of passed on tax to build a new city hall does the city get any direct allocation from the contractor's taxes taken by the state no there is absolutely no feedback the tax the contractor would pay the tax to the state and there would be no feedback to the city of Butte or to any of these irrigation districts there's no identification of these funds that the federal government is concerned about the city would be in identically the same position as the federal government also the other rule of we would submit of Fresno County case that the contractors would be no worse off than others similarly situated the contractors for all for the state of Montana all of these myriad cities irrigation districts etc. are all in the same position we respectfully submit and reserve the rest of the time that the lower court's judgment is there before you sit down I just want to get one thing that maybe Justice Franklin has already asked you take an irrigation district as an example I think you indicated the burden of the tax might fall on the private property owners that form the district yes it would well would that be true if there were no default in the contract wouldn't it just be an extra charge to the contractor and therefore I could be borne by the cost let's assume it was a $100,000 dam your honor to control some flood waters that was going to come out of this creek and maybe inundate there would be a bond the money would be raised the construction would be completed and it would cost how would the money be raised to pay the hundred thousand there had to be a bond in other words there had to be a bond tax free part sold to the public yes well then the cost wouldn't be borne by the property owner oh yes and then the cost of it would become a lien upon the property and then he'd have to pay it off say over ten years oh I see that would be just an advance the bonds would be have to be paid off to whoever owned the bonds very well Mr. Smith Mr. Chief Justice may it please the court in our view the starting point of analysis of any intergovernmental immunity question must of course be this court celebrated decision in McCullough versus Maryland law there the state imposed a tax on the issuance of notes by any bank established without authority from the state the only bank that fit that description was the bank of the United States and this court speaking through the great chief justice struck down that tax on the authority of article six of the constitution the so-called supremacy clause which declares that this constitution and the laws of the United States shall be the supreme laws of the law of the land the core holding of McCulloch is that the states and localities cannot directly tax the United States or impose taxes the legal incidence of which falls upon the United States but there is a corollary tax immunity principle that the court has derived from McCulloch the so-called discrimination principle which is at issue here and that is that a tax may be invalid even though it does not fall directly upon the United States if it operates so as to discriminate against the government or those with whom it deals and two terms ago in United States versus County of Fresno the court reaffirmed this aspect of the teaching of McCulloch the County of Fresno involved a county tax on possessory interest of those who leased improvements in tax exempt land the court upheld the tax on the federal lessees of the United States Forest Service and in so holding the court observed that federal lessees were no worse off under California tax laws than those who rented houses in the private sector the fact that the private lessees were also subject to the tax albeit indirectly through their rent meant that the tax in the court's view did not threaten to destroy the federal function so as to run afoul of the policies underlying the the critical statement in our view of what the court did in the county of Fresno was set out at page 462 of volume 429 the court said the rule to be derived from the court's more recent decisions then is that the economic burden on a federal function of a state tax imposed on those who deal with the federal government does not render the tax unconstitutional so long as the tax is imposed equally on the other similarly situated constituents of the state before you proceed just so I'm sure I can fully follow and understand your argument do you rely or are you going to rely at all on that part of the Judge East's reasoning that has the amic guy so stirred up no the Judge East I think as Mr. Poore pointed out stated in part that he thought that one of the problems with this tax is that the federal government didn't get any of its money but the state did well the state tax of course the federal government is not going to get any money and in fact carried to its logical or illogical conclusion depending upon your view it would undermine much of what the court has done since Alabama versus King and Boozer exactly right and we don't rely on that we don't rely on that at all what we rely on is the distinction between the private contractors and the and the public contractors exactly applying the rule of County Fresno as I extracted it from the court's opinion we submit that the Montana taxed issue in this case is invalid and cannot pass constitutional muster it is a tax as has already been described of one percent of gross receipts from public contracts and the statute further defines public contractor as quote any person who enters into a contract for performing all public construction work in the state with the federal government state of Montana or with any other public board body commission or agency authorized to let or award contracts for any public work when the contract cost exceeds $1,000 to buy its terms the Montana statute applies a tax to those contractors who perform services for the federal government but a contractor who performs the same services for a private party is not subject to the tax in our view this tax is therefore not and to you harken back to what the court said in County of Fresno quote imposed equally on the other similarly situated constituents of the state end of quote because federal contractors are unlike the California unlike the Forest Service lessees in County of Fresno worse off than their counterparts who work in the private sector the private sector people don't pay the tax the public contractors do do you concede don't you that people other than federal contractors are liable for the tax absolutely we do public contractors include contractors who work for the state and contractors who work for these local localities what if the tax were made applicable as the tax in Alabama versus King and Boozer was to all contractors but had the same exemption here for contracts under $1,000 and the federal government came in and said it is in fact discriminatory against us because we never enter into any contracts that are under under $1,000 and many private individuals do I suppose that I suppose it would really depend on the evidence I mean that's not this case I mean it would seem it would seem to me supposing the federal government were able to make out its claim that it never did enter into any contracts under $1,000 yes but I think Mr. Justice it would depend also on what kind of contracts in the private sector or you know in the non-federal sector were let for more than $1,000 well supposing one was let for $900 one for $1,100 they were very much the same so one was a little bigger than the other no no no you misunderstand what I was trying to say in other words the fact that I think that the fact that the federal government didn't let any contracts for less than $1,000 wouldn't carry the day for the discrimination case it would depend in part I think as to how the tax how the tax operated in the non-federal sphere and there were a lot of there were a lot of private contracts for less than $1,000 you concede then that there may be some discriminatory impact upon the federal government that is not felt by private entities similarly situated if you would allow a line to be drawn $1,000 I suppose I do but it seems to us that the point that we think is critical here is the fact that a very law you know in our view a very significant group is excluded from the operation of the tax it's not done in terms of in terms of you know dollars but rather it's done in terms of the fact that private private contractors are simply excluded from the tax Mr. Poor has painted a picture at the beginning of his argument which I must I must tell the court is really not borne out by the record at all I mean there really is nothing in the record that suggests that there are there is no private construction activity in Montana he didn't say that Mr. Poor no he didn't say that he said it was moderate that there was or that there was a moderate amount the record really doesn't talk about how much the relative volumes of private versus public construction work exists in Montana I think we have to take it on take the statute on it but say well isn't the burden on you then to show that it's discriminatory well we think that we have made at that burden by the fact that by the fact that the federal government in fact to the extent that there are statistics in the record Mr. Justice we think that they demonstrate a large amount of federal activity don't you also have to have to show a very small amount a very large amount of private activity if Mr. Poor's version is correct there just isn't too much private contracting on a large scale done in Montana it's either done by the state or by the federal government and therefore the state was justified in lumping together these entities and saying that they were going to have to pay a tax whereas contractors employed by private entities were just kind of on a much lesser scale and could be treated differently well I think that the statistics really sort of refuse that simply because if I may refer to the courts to page 5 footnote 3 of our brief we state here the record indicates that federal projects accounts for at least 65.8% of the amount of gross receipts tax collected and for at least 57.2% of the balance retained after credit however these figures do not include all federal projects in fact there are a number of state projects that are funded by the federal government so in effect the federal government that could have been true in King and Boozer too in fact it may well be I think that it seems to us that under the rule of the county of Fresno that the court we view that case as establishing a rule that requires the court to scrutinize a state statute and to look at it and say are all similarly situated constituents of the state taxed equally and in this particular case it leaps out from the page the fact that private contrasting activity is not subject to the tax and it seems in Fresno the court says that you need a political check against the abuse and Mr. Poore's answer to your claim is that the numerous municipal corporations and their constituents form a political check I think that the fact that the federal government may be joined or that the tax base may include let me back up for a moment of course if you have a tax that's only on federal contracting activity it's very plain that that falls on the wrong side of the line now if you start adding to that tax base let's say here state contractors we would say that as we point out in the brief and further detail that really doesn't change the picture dramatically or from a constitutional point of view because of the fact that these taxes are sort of charged by the state but in effect the contractor charges them back to the state so in other words it seems to me that his case or the state's case if it has to stand and fall or fall on the addition of these local contracting activities and it seems to me it really depends upon your perspective if you want to say I don't think that the record here demonstrates or that it really can be demonstrated in any logical sort of way as to what kind of political check the local contracting activity would constitute to protect the federal government I prefer to view it from the other side of the spectrum and say that a significant amount of contracting activity which I think really has to be conceded is similarly situated I don't think that the state really seriously argues here as indeed I don't think it can that private contracting activity is not similarly situated in fact in QS if I may just refer to the fact that the rationale of the Montana Supreme Court offers four different reasons for why it thought that private
